chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Nahdi from Muhammad ibn Khalid from Isma'il ibn Abd al-Khalic who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We send dirhams with a specific exchange rate (sarf) to Ahwaz, so they buy goods for us with them, and then he writes [a contract/account]. When he sells them, an exchange rate is applied to them. If we sell them, it is upon us to mention to him the exchange rate of the dirhams in the murabahah [profit-sharing/trading partnership], which will suffice for us regarding that. He said: 'No, rather if it is murabahah, inform him of that; and if it is musawamah [bargaining/fixed price], there is no harm.'

key_terms.الْأَهْوَازُ: Ahwaz, a city in Khuzestan, Iran, used here as a trade destination
key_terms.الْمُرَابَحَةُ: Murabahah, a type of profit-sharing or trading partnership
key_terms.الْمُسَاوَمَةُ: Musawamah, a sale by bargaining with a fixed price

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between murabahah and musawamah in Shia commercial jurisprudence regarding currency exchange?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the transparency requirements in trade partnerships, distinguishing between *murabahah* (cost-plus sale) and *musawamah* (bargaining). He mandates that for *murabahah*, the initial currency exchange rate (*sarf*) of the capital sent must be explicitly communicated to ensure fairness, whereas in *musawamah*, such strict accounting is not obligatory. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on preventing *gharar* (uncertainty) and ensuring informed consent in financial transactions.
